# The Infinite Playoff

## I.

The office had been a dentist's before whoever had it last, and whoever had it last had not bothered to remove the panoramic X-ray unit bolted to the wall, so it hung there above the filing cabinets like the arm of some decommissioned robot, its cone aimed at the place where a patient's jaw would have been. Garrett had draped his jacket over it the first night. By the third week he no longer noticed it. By the fifth week he had begun talking to it—not words exactly, but the small acknowledging sounds a man makes to a dog that has settled at his feet and requires nothing.

The Lancaster County Commissioner's Panel for Competitive Integrity had given him a desk, a key, a per diem of forty-one dollars, and seventeen boxes of scorebooks spanning three seasons of the Allegheny Mountain League. His mandate was narrow: examine the Torrington Raptors' home-and-away scoring records for statistical evidence of point-shaving, produce a report, collect his fee, go home. He was the fourth person they'd hired. The first three had produced equivocal findings. Garrett was not equivocal. Garrett was the kind of man whose graduate advisor at Penn State had once told him, with something between admiration and clinical concern, that he had "a talent for seeing patterns the way other people see color—involuntarily, and everywhere."

He had not thought of Dr. Meszáros in years. He did not think of him now. He thought only of the scorebook open on the desk in front of him, the home book from July 14th, a Tuesday night game between the Raptors and the visiting Canandaigua Rivermen, and the entry in the bottom of the third inning that read, in the scorer's crabbed but legible hand: *Moye, D. — 6-4-3. GDP.*

Declan Moye. Left-handed utility player. Career .231 hitter, which was generous because it included a fourteen-game stretch in June where he'd gone 11-for-31 against the weakest pitching rotation in the league. Moye grounding into a double play in the third was not interesting. Moye grounding into a double play in the third, with a runner on first and no outs, was the kind of thing that happened four hundred times a season in the Allegheny Mountain League, because the Allegheny Mountain League was where the soft ground balls of other men's failed ambitions went to die.

What was interesting was the visiting scorer's book for the same game, the same inning, the same at-bat, which read: *Moye, D. — 1B, LD to RF.*

A line-drive single to right.

Garrett set the books side by side. He adjusted the desk lamp. The home book was a standard Wilson looseleaf, the kind every league scorer used, its cover the color of dried blood. The visiting book was identical in format but slightly newer, its spine less cracked, the pages holding their whiteness the way pages do when they haven't been thumbed through by many hands. Both bore the official signatures: home scorer Randall Teague, visiting scorer Patricia Chun. Both had been filed with the league office within the mandated seventy-two-hour window, confirmed by the date stamps on their back covers—July 17th for Teague's, July 16th for Chun's.

He checked the ink. Teague used a blue ballpoint, fine-tip, probably a Pilot G-2, the kind of pen that left faint grooves in the paper you could feel with a fingernail. Garrett felt them. They were there. Chun used black ink, slightly thicker, and her handwriting was the better of the two—trained, almost calligraphic, the product of a generation that still understood penmanship as a form of respect.

Both entries were originals. He could see where Chun's pen had paused at the start of the M in Moye, a tiny bead of ink pooling at the top of the letter's first stroke, the way ink pools when a person thinks for a microsecond before committing to the next word. You couldn't fake that. You couldn't fake the coffee ring on the bottom right corner of Teague's page, either—a perfect brown circle, slightly darker on its southern edge where the mug had tipped, the paper beneath it faintly warped from the moisture. The ring overlapped the box-score column for the seventh inning. Someone had been drinking coffee and watching the seventh inning and had set down their mug and not thought about it again, and now the ring was there like a fossil, a record of the unimportant thing that happened next to the other thing that also happened, or didn't happen, or happened differently depending on which book you believed.

He pulled the next game. July 18th. Home and away books agreed through five innings, then diverged: in the home book, the Raptors' starting pitcher left the mound in the top of the sixth with what the notation described as an apparent forearm strain. In the visiting book, the same pitcher threw a complete game, seven innings, giving up three earned runs on six hits. Final score in the home book: 4–2, Raptors. Final score in the visiting book: 3–1, Rivermen. Two different outcomes for a game played on the same field on the same night in front of whatever three hundred people had driven out to Torrington Municipal to watch minor league baseball under the lights.

He pulled July 22nd. August 1st. August 9th. The pattern was not in every game. It was not even in most games. It was in perhaps one game out of every six or seven, and the divergences were not always dramatic—sometimes just a single at-bat, a stolen base that appeared in one book and not the other, a pitching change that happened in the sixth in one record and the seventh in another. But August 19th was dramatic. In the home book, the game ended in the ninth, a walk-off double by the Raptors' third baseman. In the visiting book, the game was suspended in the seventh inning due to rain. The notation read: *Game suspended, 7th, rain. Not completed per AML Rule 4.12(a)(3).* The visiting scorer had even recorded the time of the suspension: 9:47 PM. The home scorer had recorded the final out at 9:52 PM. Five minutes apart. In one version, a man hit a double and his teammates rushed the field. In the other, someone looked at the sky and called it off, and everyone went home.

Garrett stood and went to the corkboard mounted above the desk—the dentist had apparently used it for appointment reminders; a single yellowed card reading *Mrs. Fenton 3:30 Tues* was still pinned to its upper left corner—and began to pin the pages. He worked methodically. Home books on the left, visiting books on the right. Red thread—he'd found a spool in the desk's middle drawer, as if someone had left it there specifically for him—connecting the corresponding games. He drew lines between the divergence points with a marker, red for outcome changes, blue for in-game discrepancies that didn't affect the recorded final score.

The web took shape.

It was not random. He could feel that in his chest before he could articulate it with his mind, the way you could feel, watching a batter, whether the swing was going to connect before the ball arrived—that fraction-of-a-second precognition that was really just the body recognizing a pattern the conscious brain hadn't yet decoded. The divergences clustered around specific game situations: close scores, late innings, runners in scoring position. They never appeared in blowouts. They never appeared in the first three innings. They appeared at exactly the moments where a single play could change the outcome—the moments where, if you were trying to make a game land on a particular number, you would need to insert a fork.

He sat down again. He picked up the July 14th home book and looked at the coffee ring and felt, rising through his sternum like a bubble of warm air, a pleasure so clean and complete that he almost laughed. This was it. This was the thing the first three investigators had missed, because they'd been looking for the usual signatures of point-shaving—anomalous betting lines, sudden changes in player performance, the crude arithmetic of someone paid to miss a free throw or ground into a double play. They'd been looking inside the games. The games were fine. The games were clean. It was the *records* that had been corrupted. Someone had built a system in which reality itself bifurcated at the points of maximum leverage, so that no single outcome could ever be established with certainty—a statistical fog bank, a permanent epistemological haze in which the question "what actually happened?" could never be answered, because there would always be two authentic, verified, officially filed answers.

It was, Garrett thought, the most beautiful piece of fraud he had ever seen.

He did not call the commissioner's panel. He did not call his contact at the league office, the deputy administrator named Wanda Goss who had given him the key and the per diem and a look of tired hope. He did not call anyone. The thought of calling someone did not, in fact, occur to him, the way the thought of sharing a meal does not occur to a man eating alone who has forgotten that meals can be shared.

He made coffee in the single-cup machine Wanda Goss had left on the filing cabinet. He drank it black, as he had since quitting sugar three years ago, which was also when he had quit gambling, which was also when he had quit the minor leagues—not the playing of them (he had quit that at twenty-four, the year his shoulder turned to paper) but the living-near-them, the auxiliary orbit of a man who had once been close enough to the real thing that he could still smell it from the stands. He had quit all of it at once, a triple amputation, and had cauterized the wounds with statistics—the pure kind, the academic kind, the kind that didn't care about outcomes but only about the beauty of the distribution itself. He had gotten clean, he told himself sometimes, though clean from what he was never quite able to specify. Clean from wanting things to come out a certain way. Clean from the sick undertow of caring whether the ball fell in or not. Clean the way a spreadsheet was clean: every cell accounted for, every formula transparent, no hidden variables.

He refilled his coffee and pulled the August box.

At 1:00 a.m., the web on the corkboard had grown to cover most of its surface, a nervous system of red and blue threads connecting thirty-one games across three months. At 2:00 a.m., he began a second corkboard, improvised from the back of the X-ray unit, pinning pages directly to its flat housing with strips of medical tape he'd found in the bottom drawer. At 3:00 a.m., he rolled up his sleeves and sat on the floor among the open boxes, cross-referencing not just the Raptors' games but every game in the league played on the same dates, because the fog—he was sure of this now—had been designed to spread: if you forked the Raptors' game, you had to account for the cascading effects on divisional standings, and that meant small adjustments to other teams' records, the way a ripple from a single dropped stone touches every edge of the pond.

The stone had been dropped in early July. He could see that now. Before July, the home and visiting books agreed. After July, they forked. Something had changed. Someone had begun.

He did not leave the office until 4:00 a.m. He locked the door behind him and walked to his car in the empty parking lot, and the August air was thick and sweet in the way that means rain is close, and the orange sodium lights turned the asphalt the color of a bruise, and he felt—driving to his motel on the county road with the windows down and the insects hitting the windshield in soft, arrhythmic detonations—the way he had felt once, a long time ago, the night he'd gone 3-for-4 in a game against Altoona with his father in the stands: like a man who had been given a problem the exact shape of his mind, so that his mind could fill it completely, with nothing left over and nothing left out.

He did not think about why that feeling frightened him. He did not think it was important to ask.

---

## II.

The September 3rd scorebook was not extraordinary. It was a Raptors home game against the Williamsport Lamplighters, a 6–3 loss notable only for a bench-clearing argument in the fourth over a check-swing call that both scorers, for once, recorded identically. Garrett had almost set it aside. But the margin of the fifth-inning page caught his eye—a notation, small, in pencil, partially erased but still legible under the desk lamp if he tilted the page to catch the light at a certain angle.

It read: *Adj. f/discrepancy: Kessel IP recalc'd per corrected entry method (see SV-14 protocol).*

SV-14 was not a real protocol. He knew this because he had invented it.

He had invented it in the spring of 2019, during his eighteen months as an independent statistical consultant to the Allegheny Mountain League's central office. The job had been unglamorous—reconciling box scores, flagging data-entry errors, building the spreadsheet architecture that the league's overburdened administrators used to compile season statistics. He had developed, during those months, a number of shorthand notations for common correction types: SV-1 through SV-8 for various categories of scoring discrepancy, SV-9 through SV-12 for statistical adjustments required when official scorers disagreed on hit-or-error calls. SV-13 he had reserved for rain-delay complications. SV-14 was his own private notation, never shared with anyone, never included in any official documentation, for a specific and somewhat arcane correction: the smoothing of innings-pitched calculations when a pitcher recorded partial outs in multiple innings and the standard rounding convention produced a total that disagreed with the cumulative box score by a margin too small to trigger a flag but large enough to cascade through downstream statistics if left uncorrected.

He had devised the method. He had devised the notation. He had used it perhaps a dozen times during his tenure, always in his own working files, always erased before the final documents were submitted. No one else in the league office had ever seen it—he was fairly sure of this, because no one else in the league office had understood the problem it was designed to solve. Wanda Goss had once asked him what all the SV codes meant, and he had explained SV-1 through SV-8 and she had stopped him there, satisfied. SV-14 was his.

And here it was, in a scorebook from a season he hadn't worked, in a hand that—

He stopped.

He tilted the page again. The pencil notation was cramped, small enough to fit in the margin without crowding the printed columns, and the letters were unremarkable—standard print, the kind of lettering that a thousand people might produce. But the numeral 7 in *SV-14* was crossed. A horizontal stroke through the vertical stem, the European convention, the way the French and the Germans wrote their sevens to distinguish them from ones.

Garrett wrote his sevens that way. He had since his first semester at Penn State, when Dr. Meszáros—Hungarian-born, trained at the Budapest University of Technology and Economics, a man who wrote every numeral with the deliberate precision of someone for whom mathematical notation was a moral act—had handed back his first problem set with a single annotation in red ink: *Your sevens and your ones are indistinguishable. Fix this, or fix your career.* Garrett had fixed it that afternoon. He had crossed his sevens ever since. It was the one affectation he'd carried out of graduate school, a small private inheritance from a man he had otherwise disappointed, and he wore it the way some men wore class rings: not thinking about it, but never taking it off.

He went to the filing cabinet where he kept his working papers—the spreadsheets and correction logs from his current investigation—and pulled a page at random. He checked his sevens. Crossed. He checked the angle of the cross-stroke. Down from left to right, approximately thirty degrees off horizontal, placed about two-thirds of the way up the vertical stem. He went back to the scorebook. The seven in *SV-14* was crossed. Down from left to right. Approximately thirty degrees. Two-thirds up.

He pulled his briefcase from under the desk and found the brown accordion file he kept there, the one labeled "Personal Reference — AML 2019" that held copies of his working papers from his time with the league office. He had kept them out of professional habit, the way accountants kept copies of completed returns—not because he expected to need them, but because a statistician who didn't keep records was like a surgeon who didn't wash his hands. He opened the file and pulled the first page and looked at the handwriting and looked at the scorebook and felt the air in the room change, not its temperature but its density, as if the space between molecules had quietly decreased.

The handwriting matched.
